query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A modest, controlled thermomechanical treatment—specifically, light cold rolling (~10–15% reduction) followed by a short, low‐temperature annealing step—will modify the dual-phase lamellar colony interfaces of the eutectic high‐entropy alloy to reduce dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations, thereby overcoming inherent room-temperature brittleness while maintaining or even increasing its strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies that currently exhibits tensile brittleness at room temperature due to dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: Perform light cold rolling (approximately 10–15% thickness reduction) to introduce a controlled level of plastic strain, followed by a short-duration annealing treatment at a temperature just below full recrystallization (e.g., 500–600°C for several minutes).
generation.conditions: Subsequent testing with standard room-temperature tensile tests in air under moderate strain rates (e.g., quasi-static loading) to reflect typical service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified internal interfaces and slightly refined lamellar spacing that become more coherent and are better able to absorb or deflect dislocations.
generation.mechanism: The controlled deformation introduces a uniform substructure that, coupled with low-temperature annealing, promotes partial recovery at the interlamellar boundaries. This process enhances the ability of the interfaces to act as sinks for dislocations, reducing stress concentrations associated with pile-ups. The subtle modification in microstructure allows for more homogeneous plastic deformation, mitigating the previously observed local overload and microcracking while retaining fine-scale microstructural features that provide strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to demonstrate significantly increased room-temperature tensile ductility (i.e., higher strain to failure) while maintaining or possibly increasing its yield and ultimate tensile strength compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies, which shows limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness.
generation.boundary: The exact magnitude of ductility improvement and strength retention/increase depends on the precise processing window; excessive annealing might lead to grain coarsening, so the optimum parameters require fine-tuning.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the optimal degree of cold work and annealing time/temperature needed to maximize interfacial improvement without compromising the fine-scale reinforcing microstructure. Further experimental calibration is necessary to pinpoint this window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same batch of the eutectic high-entropy alloy: one set to undergo the proposed light cold rolling (~10–15% reduction) followed by low-temperature annealing (500–600°C for a short duration), and a control set with no such treatment. Perform room-temperature tensile tests using identical strain rate protocols for both sets.
measurements: Fractography to assess microcracking and dislocation pile-up patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase (e.g., >10% improvement) in plastic strain to failure without a corresponding decrease in yield or tensile strength compared to the untreated control, or if increased microcracking at internal boundaries is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.
